newsitem.title: USA: Scientists celebrate Pathfinder's week on Mars.
newsitem.headline: Scientists celebrate Pathfinder's week on Mars.

text.p: The Mars Pathfinder mission hit a fresh snag on Friday, but that did not stop scientists from celebrating the first week's historic exploration of the Red Planet.

Mission manager Richard Cook said a miscue in communications between Earth and the spacecraft caused the star of the show, the little buggy Sojourner, to remain stuck up against a rock following Thursday's fender-bender.

Cook said the rover failed to receive its new instructions because mission controllers at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory here turned on Pathfinder's receiver 11 minutes after commands were sent via the Deep Space Network.
During the fender-bender incident, the Sojourner backed into the rock dubbed "Yogi" too fast and one of its rear wheels rode up onto the rock's surface.
Scientists want it to drive away from "Yogi," and then reposition itself against the rock and analyse it with its alpha proton X-ray spectrometer.
Those instructions would be sent later on Friday, said Cook, who called the communications glitch "a minor thing and nothing to worry about."
"We just didn't get as much accomplished as we would have liked. As the team joked; on the seventh day we decided to rest," Cook said.

Image scientists on Friday displayed a magnificent three-dimensional "Monster Pan" -- a 180-degree panorama of the Martian landscape stretching from the lander to the horizon. Journalists attending the press briefing wore special glasses to view the scene.
Cook said the photograph would be topped next week when NASA shows off its Mars "Gallery Pan," a 360-degree Panoramic view of the Martian surface.
The rover will finish its primary mission on Saturday but Pathfinder Project Director Tony Spear announced that NASA had given the team funding to extend the mission for one year.

Geologist Larry Soderblom of the United States Geological Survey said the Pathfinder landing site was a geologist's dream because the winds on Mars were scouring the red Martian soil, pushing it into the sub-surface and revealing the ancient Martian rocks that could contain evidence of early, primitive life.
"The Martian sands of time are being drawn back," he said.
Norman Haynes, the Jet Propulsion Laboratory's Director of Mars Projects, said the Pathfinder team had accomplished four major goals.

They had proved that the new policy of "faster, better, cheaper" worked, taking Pathfinder to Mars and operating it there for slightly less than the allotted budget of $196 million, a fraction of the cost of previous space missions.

They also proved that an alternative landing mechanism for Mars, giant airbags, worked; they demonstrated that roving vehicles could operate on Mars -- an essential for future manned exploration -- and they returned a huge amount of scientific data that came as an added bonus because the flight was essentially an engineering exercise to prove that all the systems worked.

Haynes said he expected a manned expedition to Mars in the second decade of the 21st century, following four more unmanned landing and five orbiting spacecraft scheduled to visit the Red Planet between now and 2005.

"This really has been a fantastic week. I have to keep slapping myself to prove I'm not dreaming," said Project Scientist Matthew Golombek, a NASA geologist in charge of the Mars Pathfinder's scientific mission.

The Pathfinder lander hit the surface of the Red Planet with a thump last Friday. Since then it has thrilled scientists and the public by providing a wealth of scientific information and stunning pictures sent back by the rover and the landing craft.

The Pathfinder has amassed a number of space firsts. It was first to deploy a parachute at supersonic speeds of 1,000 mph (1,609 kph), first to use airbags to cushion its landing and to use a self-righting craft that signalled back to Earth it had arrived just three minutes after touch-down.

In the past week the rover has analysed a Martian rock that showed the Red Planet to be a solar twin of Earth because of its almost identical similarity to rocks on our own planet, while pictures taken on the lander by a three-dimensional camera provided proof that there was water on Mars, and possibly a much warmer atmosphere. These are two of the vital ingredients to promoting life on the planet.
